CausalChain: Chronic liver injury and inflammation → Excess TGF‐β production → Downregulation of TGF‐βR3 in HCC cells → Enhanced activation of the complement system and increased C5a generation → Activation of ERK1/2 and induction of EMT in tumor cells → Upregulation of immune checkpoint molecules and establishment of an immunosuppressive TME → Increased tumor invasiveness and immune evasion
Hypothesis: Downregulation of TGF‐βR3 in HCC cells amplifies complement C5a production, which drives EMT and immune checkpoint upregulation; thus, inhibiting the TGF‐βR3/C5a axis could mitigate tumor aggressiveness and restore effective anti-tumor immunity in HCC.
Abstract: We propose that in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) a previously underappreciated axis, linking aberrant TGF‐β signaling with dysregulated complement activation, drives tumor progression and immune evasion. In particular, downregulation of the type III TGF‐β receptor (TGF‐βR3) in HCC cells may result in enhanced production of the complement component C5a, which in turn promotes epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) through activation of downstream signaling such as ERK1/2. This cascade not only facilitates tumor invasiveness and metastasis but also contributes to an immunosuppressive microenvironment (via upregulation of immune checkpoint molecules) that hinders effective anti‐tumor T cell responses. Therefore, targeting the TGF‐βR3/C5a axis may restore immune surveillance and attenuate HCC progression.
